translation: The ancients, in the pulse, differentiated internal and external injury at the Renying and Qikou [positions]. If the Renying pulse is larger than the Qikou, it is external injury; if the Qikou pulse is larger than the Renying, it is internal injury. This differentiation is certainly correct, but its explanation has something incomplete. External contraction of wind-cold are all patterns of excess; this is the guest pathogen that comes from before [externally]. Its disease must be seen in the left hand; the left hand governs the surface and travels the yang twenty-five measures. Internal injury of food and drink, and immoderate food and drink and immoderate toil, are all diseases of insufficiency; they must be seen in the right hand; the right hand governs the interior and travels the yin twenty-five measures. Hence in external contraction of cold pathogen, then the Renying pulse of the left cun [position] alone is floating and tight; pressed, it is surging, large, and tight — urgent beyond [that of] the string [pulse]. This is the pulse of the foot-taiyang cold-water; pressed, it is surging, large, and forceful, and within, the heart-fire pulse of the hand-shaoyin is seen. Ding and Ren unite, and within there appears surging and large — this is the cold-damage pulse. If there is external contraction of the wind pathogen, then the Renying pulse is moderate and larger than the Qikou by double or two or three times. In internal injury of food and drink, then the Qikou pulse of the right cun is larger than the Renying by one-fold; in heavy injury, if the excess lies in the shaoyin, then by two-fold; if in the taiyin, then by three-fold. This is the pulse of internal injury of food and drink. If food and drink are immoderate and toil is excessive, then the heart pulse is seen transformed at the Qikou; this is heart-fire punishing the lung, and its liver-wood also, carrying the force of heart-fire, comes likewise to oppress the lung. The Classic states: "[He who] insults what does not conquer [him]... " — "insulating the one lacking fear." Hence the Qikou pulse is urgent, large, astringent, and rapid, and at times it is one-ternion with astringency. The astringent [pulse] is the root pulse of the lung; the ternion [intermittent] pulse means the Original Qi is not connecting [through], the pulse of insufficiency of the spleen and stomach; surging, large, and rapid — heart pulse punishing the lung; urgent — the liver-wood, carrying heart-fire, instead overcomes the lung-metal. If the toil is not severe, then only the right guan spleen pulse is large and rapid — called solely larger than the five pulses — and within the rapid [beat] appears moderate, at times one-ternion. If food and drink are immoderate and cold and warmth are lost in their place, then first the stomach pulse of the right guan is damaged; when weak in the extreme it becomes hidden and unseen, with only the spleen pulse's large rapidity appearing within, slightly moderate, at times one-ternion. If stagnant food is undigested, then only the right guan pulse alone is deep and slippery. The Classic states: "A slippery pulse means there is stagnant food." Using this to differentiate, is it not clear and easy to see? But I only fear that in mountain villages, where there are suddenly no physicians, how can diagnosis by pulse be carried out? Therefore I will also speak the symptoms to differentiate them.
